concepts.label: ethernet-service
concepts.gloss: An Ethernet service (EVC / E-LAN) representing a carrier-managed Layer‑2 virtual connection that ties together one or more customer UNIs into a single Ethernet broadcast/multicast domain and carries one or more L2 segments and service attributes across the provider network.
concepts.example: ACME-ELAN (3 UNIs, any-to-any) is an ethernet-service that interconnects UNI-HQ, UNI-DC and UNI-Branch in an any-to-any E‑LAN so frames on a carried VLAN are delivered between any pair of those UNIs.

concepts.label: UNI
concepts.gloss: A UNI (User Network Interface) is the customer-facing access attachment point on the provider edge where an Ethernet service terminates and where per‑UNI service parameters (bandwidth profiles, MAC learning, vendor attributes, etc.) are applied.
concepts.example: UNI-HQ is a UNI instance of the ACME-ELAN service where the provider applies the BWP-200/50 profile, MAC learning policy and any vendor-specific attributes for traffic entering and leaving the customer site.

concepts.label: EVC-endpoint
concepts.gloss: An EVC-endpoint (service endpoint) is the logical endpoint of an Ethernet service located at a specific UNI that identifies the attachment/port and role of that UNI within the EVC for forwarding and service mapping purposes.
concepts.example: EP-HQ is the EVC-endpoint at UNI-HQ representing the ACME-ELAN attachment point used to receive and transmit frames for that service from the HQ site.

concepts.label: network-segment
concepts.gloss: A network-segment is a Layer‑2 broadcast/multicast domain carried by the Ethernet service (typically represented as a CE VLAN or VLAN ID) that groups customer MACs and traffic within the EVC.
concepts.example: CE-VLAN 200 is a network-segment carried by the ACME-ELAN so that devices tagged with VLAN 200 at UNI-HQ, UNI-DC and UNI-Branch share the same L2 broadcast domain across the service.

concepts.label: bandwidth-profile
concepts.gloss: A bandwidth-profile is a rate control profile applied at a UNI that specifies how traffic for the service is policed or shaped (e.g., committed and excess rates) for that attachment point.
concepts.example: BWP-200/50 applied at UNI-HQ limits the ACME-ELAN traffic from that UNI to a committed rate of 200 (units as defined by the operator) with an excess allowance of 50, thereby controlling the UNI's contribution to the service traffic.

concepts.label: class-of-service
concepts.gloss: A class-of-service is a service-level traffic treatment designation attached to the Ethernet service that defines priority, queuing and forwarding behavior (for example, real‑time vs best‑effort) for traffic in the EVC.
concepts.example: CoS-H (real-time) is assigned on the ACME-ELAN to carry voice traffic with higher priority, while CoS-L (best-effort) is used for normal data traffic on the same service.

concepts.label: MAC-learning
concepts.gloss: MAC-learning denotes the source‑MAC learning behavior configured at a UNI that controls whether the provider edge dynamically learns MAC addresses from customer frames to populate forwarding state for the EVC.
concepts.example: The instance 'dynamic learning @UNI-HQ' indicates MAC-learning is enabled at UNI-HQ so the provider edge will learn EP-HQ's source MACs and use them to forward frames within the ACME-ELAN.

concepts.label: service-mtu
concepts.gloss: Service-mtu is the maximum frame payload/packet size allowed across the Ethernet service (the MTU advertised/enforced within the EVC) that determines the largest frame that can be forwarded end‑to‑end by the service.
concepts.example: MTU 9100 configured on the ACME-ELAN allows jumbo frames up to 9100 bytes to be exchanged between UNI-HQ, UNI-DC and UNI-Branch over that service.

concepts.label: service-availability
concepts.gloss: Service-availability is an assurance objective that specifies the target uptime or availability SLO for the Ethernet service (the acceptable percentage of time the EVC must be operational over a measurement period).
concepts.example: A 99.99% objective for the ACME-ELAN means the provider commits to keeping the EVC available for that percentage of time (roughly allowing about 52.56 minutes of downtime per year).

concepts.label: x-mef-attr-5
concepts.gloss: x-mef-attr-5 is a vendor‑specific (opaque) attribute attached to a UNI used to carry proprietary or implementation‑specific configuration data whose meaning is outside the standard model and interpreted by the vendor's equipment or translator.
concepts.example: The instance 'x-mef-attr-5=0x3 at UNI-HQ' indicates a vendor-specific flag/value (0x3) has been set on UNI-HQ and must be interpreted by the vendor's device or provisioning adapter when configuring that UNI for the service.
